name: 困
title: Learning from Oppression (Kùn): keep room for judgment and action under constraint
plainSummary: When circumstances restrict you, identify the real obstacles and available support; you need not prove yourself by acting tough or explaining yourself repeatedly.
introduction: Kun does not reduce hardship to a breezy instruction to “look on the bright side.” Dead wood, stones, thorns, vines, and ancient punishments depict different situations in which action is blocked, help arrives late, or words are not believed. Reading requires taking limits seriously without treating suffering as a qualification worth actively pursuing.
identityText: 困 is hexagram 47 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with the symbol ䷮. Its lower trigram is 坎☵ and its upper trigram is 兑☱, traditionally associated with water and lake respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初六, 九二, 六三, 九四, 九五, 上六. A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Nine and six identify yang and yin in the line labels; they do not add extra lines.

guaci.label: The judgment
guaci.classical: 困：亨，貞大人吉，无咎，有言不信。
paragraphs: Legge understands Kun as a cramped, pressured condition in which one cannot move freely. “Words are not believed” reminds us that speaking may not work. It does not mean that someone describing hardship must be lying, or that a person in difficulty should always remain silent.

For modern study, begin by distinguishing what is happening: a lack of resources, restrictive rules, misunderstanding, or support that cannot arrive? Making the problem specific helps identify assistance that can actually work. The ancient terms for favorable progress and good fortune cannot guarantee that suffering will be rewarded.
guaci.classicalTranslation: Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constraint: favorable progress. Constancy brings good fortune for a great person, without blame. Words are spoken but not believed.

tenWings.label: Interpretation in the Ten Wings
paragraphs: The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the Yi Zhuan, the commentaries usually called the “Ten Wings.” Here their explanations are kept distinct from the judgment and line texts, before turning to modern applications for study.

The Commentary on the Judgment speaks of not losing one’s proper ground under constraint and criticizes reliance on mere talk. The Commentary on the Images depicts a lake without water and includes 致命遂志, an ancient ethical expression about giving one’s life to fulfill one’s purpose. This concerns holding to one’s resolve in extreme circumstances; it should not be casually turned into an everyday slogan.

This article does not turn that expression into a demand for self-sacrifice, self-harm, enduring abuse, or refusing help. For ordinary study today, it takes only the ideas of preserving principles and recognizing room for action. Safety and practical support deserve serious protection.

# Learning from Oppression (Kùn): keep room for judgment and action under constraint

When circumstances restrict you, identify the real obstacles and available support; you need not prove yourself by acting tough or explaining yourself repeatedly.

Kun does not reduce hardship to a breezy instruction to “look on the bright side.” Dead wood, stones, thorns, vines, and ancient punishments depict different situations in which action is blocked, help arrives late, or words are not believed. Reading requires taking limits seriously without treating suffering as a qualification worth actively pursuing.

困 is hexagram 47 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with the symbol ䷮. Its lower trigram is 坎☵ and its upper trigram is 兑☱, traditionally associated with water and lake respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初六, 九二, 六三, 九四, 九五, 上六. A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Nine and six identify yang and yin in the line labels; they do not add extra lines.

Line structure (bottom to top): 0 1 0 1 1 0

Six-line figure, displayed top to bottom; line numbering starts at the bottom.

```text
━━━━ ━━━━  上六
━━━━━━━━━  九五
━━━━━━━━━  九四
━━━━ ━━━━  六三

```

## The judgment

困：亨，貞大人吉，无咎，有言不信。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constraint: favorable progress. Constancy brings good fortune for a great person, without blame. Words are spoken but not believed.

Legge understands Kun as a cramped, pressured condition in which one cannot move freely. “Words are not believed” reminds us that speaking may not work. It does not mean that someone describing hardship must be lying, or that a person in difficulty should always remain silent.

For modern study, begin by distinguishing what is happening: a lack of resources, restrictive rules, misunderstanding, or support that cannot arrive? Making the problem specific helps identify assistance that can actually work. The ancient terms for favorable progress and good fortune cannot guarantee that suffering will be rewarded.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Interpretation in the Ten Wings

The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the Yi Zhuan, the commentaries usually called the “Ten Wings.” Here their explanations are kept distinct from the judgment and line texts, before turning to modern applications for study.

The Commentary on the Judgment speaks of not losing one’s proper ground under constraint and criticizes reliance on mere talk. The Commentary on the Images depicts a lake without water and includes 致命遂志, an ancient ethical expression about giving one’s life to fulfill one’s purpose. This concerns holding to one’s resolve in extreme circumstances; it should not be casually turned into an everyday slogan.

This article does not turn that expression into a demand for self-sacrifice, self-harm, enduring abuse, or refusing help. For ordinary study today, it takes only the ideas of preserving principles and recognizing room for action. Safety and practical support deserve serious protection.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [hon-sep](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-change/)

## 初六 · Acknowledge the isolation of prolonged constraint

臀困于株木，入于幽谷，三歲不覿。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: The buttocks are constrained by a tree stump. Entering a dark valley, one sees no one for three years.

The image is heavy: one’s seat is obstructed by dead wood, one enters a dark valley, and for three years sees no one. Legge preserves the sense of having no way out. It should not be lightly recast as advice to rest.

If a difficulty has lasted a long time, share what you know with someone trustworthy who can help check what choices remain. Three years is language within the line, not a real-life requirement to wait alone for that period.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九二 · Material provision can coexist with constraint

困于酒食，朱紱方來，利用亨祀，征凶，无咎。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constrained amid wine and food; vermilion knee-coverings are approaching. Sacrificial offerings are appropriate. Advancing is unfavorable; no blame.

Being constrained amid wine and food is not a simple account of hunger. It is followed by a vermilion knee-covering associated with rank and by sacrifice. Legge develops his explanation through office, support, and the timing of action.

Someone who appears materially comfortable may still lack autonomy or appropriate support. Understanding hardship requires listening to the particular circumstances. “You already have so much” does not disqualify a person from describing their difficulty.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 六三 · Do not lean on something that causes further harm

困于石，據于蒺藜，入于其宮，不見其妻，凶。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constrained by stone, leaning on thorns. Entering one’s house, one does not see one’s wife. Unfavorable.

A stone blocks the way, the support at hand is thorny, and returning home brings another absence. Legge reads a predicament combining obstruction with reliance on the wrong support.

When seeking help, also ask whether that help introduces new control or harm. The missing wife belongs to an ancient scene; it cannot establish that a present-day partner will leave or betray someone.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九四 · Conditions along the way may delay help

來徐徐，困于金轝，吝，有終。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Coming slowly, constrained by a metal carriage. Embarrassment, but there is an eventual conclusion.

The arrival is slow, and a metal carriage creates constraint. Legge explains this as someone wanting to help another but meeting obstacles. The better ending does not erase the delay along the way.

When promising assistance, explain what you can do and when you can respond. If you cannot arrive yet, provide an honest update rather than leaving silence for the person who most needs to know.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九五 · Recognize a harsh setting without romanticizing injury

劓刖，困于赤紱，乃徐有說，利用祭祀。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Nose and feet cut off; constrained by red knee-coverings. Then relief gradually comes. Sacrificial offerings are appropriate.

劓刖 refers to ancient punishments involving cutting off the nose and feet; the red knee-covering points to official dress. Legge preserves the images of injury and constraint and acknowledges that his commentary’s explanation may not be satisfactory.

A modern analogy cannot require someone to accept physical injury as proof of resolve. Faced with clear injustice or harm, seek practical protection and appropriate help. “Relief gradually comes” is not a guarantee that endurance alone will improve things.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 上六 · Reconsider the judgment that makes movement seem impossible

困于葛藟，于臲卼，曰動悔。有悔，征吉。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constrained by vines and on unsteady ground, one says, “Moving will bring regret.” With regret and reconsideration, going forward is favorable.

Vines entangle, the footing is unsteady, and there is fear that any movement will bring regret. Legge understands the final phrase as the possibility of a new direction for action after reflecting on earlier mistakes.

Break “I have no choice” into specific limitations and check them one by one. Some constraints genuinely cannot change immediately; others can be reassessed through information, support, or a small-scale trial.

Sources: [zhouyi-47](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/困&oldid=10647032), [legge1882-47](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## A volunteer project meets several constraints

Original modern scenario

A volunteer is organizing exhibition materials but cannot obtain key files or confirm when the coordinator will reply. He first records the missing materials, completed work, and items awaiting action. He does not keep promising that the original deadline will certainly be met.

Another member offers help but has limited time. They clarify responsibilities and tell the group which stages still cannot move forward. They value that support without exaggerating it into a solution to every problem.

If the necessary conditions remain unavailable, they will adjust the scope or pause that portion of the work. Kun’s modern application is to identify limits honestly and protect room for action, rather than proving responsibility through unlimited exhaustion.

## Avoiding misreadings

- Kun is not a moral judgment on people in difficulty, nor a promise that endurance will be rewarded. Seeking help, leaving a harmful situation, or adjusting a goal does not mean abandoning principles.

- Ancient punishments, the expression 致命遂志, and time spans in the text cannot provide reasons to harm oneself, assessments of health, or predictions of disaster.

## Three exercises

1. Separate the predicament into factual constraints, unverified worries, and matters you can still decide.

2. Write down one specific need for support so that a trustworthy person knows what would actually help.

3. Check whether a commitment exceeds current conditions; adjust it promptly and explain if necessary.

## Related reading

Jing — The Well (hexagram-48): Kun asks how to retain judgment under constraint; Jing asks how dependable support is maintained and actually used. The former reveals what is lacking; the latter checks whether resources really reach those who need them.

When reading Kun, ask: what support would actually reduce the constraints before me, rather than merely make me seem better at enduring them?

## Textual note

The third line uses the base text’s listed variant 藜; the fourth uses the variant 徐徐 and retains 轝. The imagery of punishment is not softened into a risk-free metaphor.
